claims.text: The starting material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has low hardness.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has low strength.
The simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi starting state lacks significant lattice distortion.
The simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi starting state lacks a secondary phase.
The lack of significant lattice distortion and secondary phases governs the low hardness and strength of the starting alloy.
Significant lattice distortion and secondary phases are typically present in other high-entropy alloys with improved mechanical properties.
Alloying or processing can introduce greater lattice distortion or a secondary phase into CoCrFeNiTi.
Greater lattice distortion produces solid-solution strengthening.
Secondary-phase precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby produce precipitation strengthening.
Introducing greater lattice distortion and secondary-phase precipitation will increase strength relative to the starting state.
Introducing greater lattice distortion and secondary-phase precipitation will increase hardness relative to the starting state.
The hypothesis is scoped to equimolar or nearly equimolar compositions tested at room temperature and quasi-static strain rates.
The detailed way in which lattice distortion and precipitation improve the properties of CoCrFeNiTi is not fully understood.
Failure of introduced lattice distortion and secondary-phase precipitation to improve hardness and strength would falsify the hypothesis.
